Hospitals do not necessarily provide lower-quality care on weekends. While some studies suggest that weekend hospitalization may lead to delayed provision of intensive procedures, elevated 1-year mortality for elderly AMI (acute myocardial infarction) patients, and differences in treatments, this does not necessarily mean that hospitals are providing lower-quality care.

In fact, research suggests that targeted financial incentives might be a more cost-effective policy response than broad regulation aimed at improving quality. This is because the existence of measurable differences in treatments raises questions about the efficacy of a single input regulation (e.g., mandated nurse staffing ratios) in enhancing the quality of weekend care.

It's also worth noting that GP hospitals (general practitioner hospitals) seem to reduce the utilization of general hospitals with respect to admissions and occupied bed days. This suggests that patients may be choosing to see their GP for primary care rather than being admitted to a general hospital.

Additionally, studies have shown that having a regular primary care clinician is associated with modest gains in interpersonal quality and no differences in content of anticipatory guidance for young children. For this age group, the benefit of having a regular clinician may primarily occur in interpersonal quality, but it does not necessarily translate to better health-related quality of life outcomes.

It's also worth mentioning that provider service networks (PSNs) have been shown to result in lower expenditures compared with HMOs (health maintenance organizations) or primary care case management in Florida's Medicaid program. PSNs generate slightly greater reductions in expenditures compared to HMOs, and are a promising model for delivering care to Medicaid enrollees.

Overall, the evidence suggests that hospitals may not necessarily provide lower-quality care on weekends, but rather there may be other factors at play, such as differences in patient selection or treatment protocols.
